doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

title: Trombone playing then and now; grandchildren like Ellington
summary: Few recordings exist, Mead studies trombone in retirement, and his grandchildren prefer Ellington.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: You must have progressed pretty quickly as a trombone player I guess, in keeping up with that company.

Well you know there weren’t a lot of recordings made. We actually have a recording from Carnegie Hall but other than that there isn’t much. I wished I did because it would be fun. I’ve asked, since I’ve retired in the last three years, I’ve actually taken up the trombone after playing it for fifty years and I actually study with a guy at the University of Vermont, Peter Bouchard, who is a classical trombonist, and I’ve certainly learned a great deal about playing the trombone and I think I’m a much better trombonist now. But you know, you’ve sure got good chops when you’re 18 and you sure don’t when you’re 69 so I don’t know. I’ve had some discussions with some trumpet players about this. And some people feel that hearing my dad play, you know, a couple hours a day every day of my life probably until I went to college, probably was the best thing that could have happened to me. And so with our own grandchildren we always have jazz on the — have a CD going. And you know what they like — and we have a pretty wide collection — and you know what they like the most?

Which is fascinating. Because I listen to a lot of hard bop, I listen to a lot of Dixieland, a lot of swing, a lot of thirties and forties stuff now and I’m even getting back into New Orleans stuff. There’s all that stuff on, and I love the big band, you know, Woody Herman and Stan Kenton. But they actually like Ellington, which I think is good.
